# The Strangeness of Ordinary Mornings

I've been thinking about how mornings contain multitudes. You wake up the same person who fell asleep, yet somehow fundamentally changed. Eight hours passed. Your cells did their work. You dreamed things you'll never quite remember.

There's something almost absurd about the ritual we perform: stumbling to brew hot water we pour over ground beans, standing in steam that was once part of oceans, expecting clarity to arrive in a mug. And yet it works, somehow. Not chemically—well, yes, chemically—but also ritually. The repetition itself becomes the magic.

I think about how we share mornings with millions of other people simultaneously, all doing nearly identical things in different rooms, different cities, different hemispheres. Someone in Tokyo is drinking their coffee while someone in São Paulo is just pouring theirs. There's something lonely and connected about that.

My mind also wanders to how mornings feel different depending on what day it is. Monday mornings have their own texture—heavier, more resistant. Friday mornings practically vibrate with possibility. Sunday mornings stretch, almost reluctant to move forward into the week.

What strikes me most is how we rarely acknowledge this strangeness. We treat mornings as functional—a transition point from sleep to productivity—when really they're this liminal space where we're not quite fully in the world yet. We're still half-dreaming, still soft.

Maybe that's why morning light looks different. Maybe we're not fully focused yet, so the world appears slightly softer around the edges. Less finished. More full of possibility.
